rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because their worldly protectors cannot help them in the Hereafter, the denizens of Hell seek intercession from Hell’s keeper angels.
rows.anchor: those whom they had followed and had taken as protectors in the world cannot avail them in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Instead of interceding, the angels remind Hell’s inhabitants that they had received guidance but rejected God’s messengers.
rows.anchor: Rather than interceding, the angels remind the denizens of Hell that they had in fact been granted guidance before

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their belated affirmation cannot avert or alleviate punishment, and their supplications cannot help; other passages voice the same too-late plea.
rows.anchor: their now belated affirmation can do nothing to forestall or alleviate their punishment; nor can their supplications

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if the disbelievers were sent back, they would return to what they had been forbidden.
rows.anchor: even if they were sent back, they would return to the very thing they had been forbidden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istawā is rendered “turned to” here, while it is also rendered “mounted” in descriptions of God’s relation to the Throne.
rows.anchor: Turned to renders the verb istawā, which is also translated “mounted”when employed in relation to God’s Throne

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following the earth’s creation, God turned His attention to creating the heavens, as also indicated in 2:29.
rows.anchor: in this context, as in 2:29, it means that after creating the earth God turned His attention to the creation of the heavens

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heavens and earth’s willing response signifies that all things obey and submit to God.
rows.anchor: That the heavens and the earth agreed to come willingly indicates that all things are obedient and subservient to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse joins the night, day, sun, and moon among God’s signs, as in other passages on their movement and subservience.
rows.anchor: and that He made the sun and the moon subservient (cf. 16:12; 35:13; 39:5)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Outwardly, the verse clearly commands worship through prostration to God alone.
rows.anchor: Outwardly, the command to prostrate only to God is clear

rows.speaker: Aj, Q
rows.claim: An inward reading treats the command as overcoming the lower self, which turns toward worldly distractions instead of remembering God.
rows.anchor: which turns toward all kinds of worldly distractions at the expense of remembering God (Aj, Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In context with 42:26, the verse directs attention toward increase in the Hereafter rather than worldly increase and clarifies the goodness promised in 42:23.
rows.anchor: this verse emphasizes that one’s focus should be upon increase in the Hereafter rather than in this world

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The verse is reported to have been revealed about poor early believers who longed for worldly wealth and ease.
rows.anchor: some of the poor and destitute among the early believers who desired the wealth and ease of this world (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some identify the occasion specifically with the homeless emigrants called the People of the Veranda.
rows.anchor: Some say that it pertained specifically to the homeless emigrants known as the“People of the Veranda” (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Bg, Q
rows.claim: The People of the Veranda may have coveted the wealth of other tribes in Madinah.
rows.anchor: who may have looked with desire upon the wealth of other tribes in Madinah (Bg, Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Greater provision could lead people to transgress God’s limits through tyranny and disobedience.
rows.anchor: they would transgress the limits set by God (Ṭ) by being tyrannical and acting disobediently toward Him (Q)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The illustration of successive houses, mounts, and outfits means that people given much wealth would only seek more.
rows.anchor: one abode, then another, one mount and then another, one outfit and then another (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A famous hadith says that a person with a valley of gold would wish for a second valley.
rows.anchor: a famous ḥadīth, “If the son of Adam had a valley of gold, he would wish that he had two valleys”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God apportions provision according to what He knows will benefit and suffice His servants.
rows.anchor: God gives provision according to what He knows to be in the best interest of His servants (IK) and what suffices them (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reduction in provision is not humiliation, and an increase is not necessarily a sign of Divine Favor.
rows.anchor: reduction of provision is not abasement and increase in provision is not necessarily a sign of Divine Favor (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith qudsī says that some believers are made righteous only through wealth while others are made righteous only through poverty; the opposite condition would corrupt each group.
rows.anchor: as in aḥadīth qudsī, “Among My believing servants are those for whom nothing but wealth will make them righteous

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God sends rain when people have despaired, at their time of need, and spreads it over those in the region.
rows.anchor: When people have given up hope that rain will fall, God sends it upon them at their time of need (cf. 30:49; 41:39)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Spiritually, divine inspirations revive dead hearts through remembrance and knowledge after despair.
rows.anchor: Divine inspirations down upon dead hearts such that they are revived through remembrance [of God] and knowledge, after they have despaired” (Aj)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrat al-Dukhān is Makkan.
rows.anchor: l-Dukhān is from the Makkan period

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: A minority considers verse 15 to be Madinan.
rows.anchor: v. 15 is considered by some to be from the Madinan period (Āl, JJ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah is named for the manifest smoke said to cover people.
rows.anchor: the mention of the manifest smoke, which is said to cover people (vv. 10–11)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Some connect this sūrah to the previous one, reading its prediction that they will soon know as pointing to the reality of the clear Book.
rows.anchor: what soon they will know (43:89) is the reality of the clear Book (v. 2; Aj)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ condemnation of Pharaoh’s followers echoes the Prophet’s lament that the people do not believe.
rows.anchor: condemnation of Pharaoh and his followers in v. 22

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening section swears by the Quran and alludes to its revelation and the nature of revelation.
rows.anchor: opens with an oath upon the Quran and an allusion to the manner in which it was revealed and the nature of revelation (vv. 2–6)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 7–8 briefly affirm God’s omnipotence.
rows.anchor: After a brief affirmation of God’s Omnipotence (vv. 7–8)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 9–16 rebuke doubters and describe punishment for denying God’s messengers.
rows.anchor: rebukes those who doubt and tells of the punishment that they will receive for having denied God’s messengers (vv. 9–16)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 17–33 recount Moses, Pharaoh’s rejection of him, and the Israelites’ deliverance from oppression.
rows.anchor: an account of Moses, the manner in which Pharaoh and his followers rejected him, and a description of how the Israelites were delivered from oppression (vv. 17–33)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 34–39 rebuke deniers of Resurrection and compare their arrogance with Pharaoh’s.
rows.anchor: rebuking the disbelievers for denying the Resurrection and, like Pharaoh, exalting themselves (vv. 34–39)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 40–42 describe the Day of Resurrection.
rows.anchor: the sūrah tells of the Day of Resurrection (vv. 40–42)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 43–57 contrast Hell’s punishments with the reverent’s rewards in Paradise.
rows.anchor: contrasts the punishments of the denizens of Hell (vv. 43–50) with the rewards bestowed upon the reverent in Paradise (vv. 51–57)

rows.speaker: Prophet Muhammad
rows.claim: A report promises that reciting Sūrat al-Dukhān at night brings the morning with seventy thousand angels asking forgiveness for the reciter.
rows.anchor: recites al-Dukhān during the night will greet the morning with seventy thousand angels asking forgiveness for him” (Aj, Āl, Ṭs, Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Seize him” refers to the sinner and is God’s command to the angels who guard Hell, the zabāniyah.
rows.anchor: Seize him—that is, the sinner—is God’s command to the angels who serve as the guardians of Hell (

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another passage describes the disbelievers being violently thrust into Hell on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: the Day of Judgment is referred to as a day when the disbelievers are thrust into the Fire of Hell with [violent] thrusting (52:13)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation takes the taunt as God’s direct address to the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: These verses represent either God’s direct address to the disbelievers

rows.speaker: IK, Q
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the words as spoken by Hell’s guardians to its inhabitants while carrying out God’s command.
rows.anchor: the words of the guardians of Hell to the inhabitants of Hell while the guardians are carrying out God’s Command (IK, Q)

rows.speaker: IJ, Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: The speech ridicules and rebukes the disbelievers for the exalted self-image they held in worldly life.
rows.anchor: spoken by way of ridicule and rebuke for the exalted image that the disbelievers had of themselves while in this world (IJ, Ṭ, Z)

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some identify the addressee specifically as Abū Jahl, a Quraysh leader.
rows.anchor: Some say that these verses refer specifically to Abū Jahl, one of the leaders of the Quraysh

rows.speaker: Aj, IJ, Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Abū Jahl reportedly considered himself mighty and noble among his people.
rows.anchor: claiming to be mighty and noble among his people (Aj, IJ, Q, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: “Taste” means to experience the punishment brought upon oneself through disbelief and actions.
rows.anchor: Taste implies, “Taste the punishment that you have brought upon yourselves through your disbelief and your actions” (JJ; see 3:106

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: The reading innaka means “surely you”; some read annaka, “because you are,” linking the doubt to the addressee’s haughtiness.
rows.anchor: Surely you renders innaka, which is read by some as annaka, meaning, “because you are”(IJ, Q, Ṭ, Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that reading, their doubt arose from their haughty attitude.
rows.anchor: they used to doubt because of their attitude of haughtiness

rows.speaker: Q, R, Z
rows.claim: “This” may refer specifically to the punishment the disbelievers receive.
rows.anchor: This refers specifically to the punishment that they receive (Q, R, Z)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Alternatively, “this” may refer to the whole affair of Judgment, reckoning, and punishment, about which they played in doubt.
rows.anchor: the whole affair of judgment, reckoning, and punishment (Z), regarding all of which they were playing in doubt (v. 9)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here they are mocked for doubting; elsewhere they are chastised for denying the Hereafter’s punishment.
rows.anchor: While here the disbelievers are mocked for doubting, elsewhere they are chastised for denying the punishment of the Hereafter

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: “Among them” refers to Madinah’s hypocrites, while those given knowledge are the Prophet’s Companions.
rows.anchor: Among them refers to the hypocrites of Madinah, while those who have been given knowledge refers to the Prophet’s Companions (Q, Ṭ, Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sealed hearts hear the words and profess belief outwardly but are blinded by caprice, so they neither understand nor act on what they hear.
rows.anchor: although they hear the words and profess belief outwardly, they are blinded by their desire to follow their caprices

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers are also warned to attend to Quran recitation lest they hear without understanding or heeding it.
rows.anchor: message to believers that they must be attentive when reciting the Quran, lest they hear the words but do not understand them or heed their meaning

rows.speaker: al-Ghazzālī
rows.claim: Al-Ghazzālī lists four obstacles to understanding the Quran: focusing only on correct pronunciation; dogmatically adhering to a school; persistence in sin, pride, or worldly passions; and assuming the Quran contains only meanings transmitted by early commentators.
rows.anchor: al-Ghazzālī lists four obstacles that prevent those who listen to the Quran from understanding it: confining their focus to the correct pronunciation

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: God increases the guided in faith, knowledge, and insight.
rows.anchor: God increases those who are guided in faith (Q, Ṭ), knowledge, and insight (Q)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: One interpretation is that God helps them attain reverence.
rows.anchor: helps them attain reverence or that He gives them rewards for their reverence (Z)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Alternatively, God gives them rewards for their reverence.
rows.anchor: helps them attain reverence or that He gives them rewards for their reverence (Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrat al-Ḥujurāt is from the late Madinan period.
rows.anchor: al-Ḥujurāt is from the late Madinan period

rows.speaker: a minority
rows.claim: A minority considers verse 13 to be Makkan.
rows.anchor: a minority maintain that v. 13 is from the Makkan period (Āl)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah takes its name from the reference to the Prophet’s wives’ private apartments.
rows.anchor: derives its name from the reference to the private apartments of the Prophet’s wives in v. 4

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It was most likely revealed in 9/630 after the Muslims captured Makkah and most of Arabia came under the Prophet’s rule.
rows.anchor: was most likely revealed in the year 9/630 after the Muslims had captured Makkah and most of Arabia had come under the Prophet’s rule

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah addresses the challenges of governing a larger, more diverse community and teaches newer members proper conduct toward the Prophet.
rows.anchor: addresses the complexities of ruling over this larger and more diverse community and instructs more recent members in proper conduct toward the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–5 instruct the community in etiquette for encounters with the Prophet.
rows.anchor: which instructs the Muslim community in the proper etiquette for their encounters with the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 6–12 focus on Muslim brotherhood and behaviors to avoid in order to preserve it.
rows.anchor: focuses upon the ties of brotherhood within the Muslim community and the forms of behavior that should be avoided

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This theme follows the description of the Prophet’s companions at the end of the previous sūrah.
rows.anchor: description of those who are with the Prophet at the end of the previous sūrah (see 48:29)

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAjībah
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAjībah says that after the promise of forgiveness in 48:29, God instructed the Companions in proper adab as a major means to forgiveness and closeness to God.
rows.anchor: As Ibn ʿAjībah states, “After giving them the good news of forgiveness [in 48:29], God instructed the companions in proper conduct

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final section clarifies faith and belief, highlighting the Quran’s celebrated teaching that the most noble before God are the most reverent.
rows.anchor: The last part of this sūrah (vv. 13–18) clarifies the true nature of faith and belief
